units.title: Adjectives and adverbs
units.summary: Adjectives describe nouns; adverbs describe verbs, adjectives and whole sentences.

cards.title: Which one?
cards.body: Adjectives describe **nouns** (a sharp rise). Adverbs describe **verbs** (rose sharply), **adjectives** (extremely expensive) and **sentences** (Surprisingly, …).
examples: There was a slight decrease.
The number decreased slightly.
Public transport is relatively cheap.

cards.title: Linking verbs take adjectives
cards.body: After **be, seem, look, sound, feel, become, remain**, use an adjective, not an adverb.
examples: The figure remained stable.
The plan sounds reasonable.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Switching between **verb + adverb** and **adjective + noun** shows grammatical range in Task 1.
examples: Sales rose dramatically in 2010, followed by a gradual decline.

practice.q: There was a ___ fall in prices.
There was a [considerably] increase in tourism.
Change to adjective + noun: 'Exports fell sharply.'
practice.a: There was a sharp fall in exports.

units.title: Comparatives and superlatives
units.summary: Comparing two things, or one with all the others.

cards.title: Short adjectives
cards.body: One syllable (and two ending in -y): **-er / the -est**. cheap → cheaper → the cheapest; busy → busier → the busiest; big → bigger → the biggest.
examples: Trains are faster than buses.
Tokyo is the largest city in the world.

cards.title: Longer adjectives
cards.body: **more / the most**; **less / the least**.
examples: Online courses are more flexible than classes.
Coal was the least popular source by 2020.

items: Both are fine; 'than I do' is formal.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Task 1 asks you to 'make comparisons where relevant' — comparatives and superlatives are essential.
examples: Germany had the highest rate of recycling, whereas Spain had the lowest.

practice.q: This was ___ result of the four countries.
Rents in the capital are ___ (expensive) than in other cities.
Electric cars are [more cheaper] to run.
It was the most [highest] figure in the table.

o: China produced the most rice of all countries.
China produced the more rice of all countries.
China produced most rice than all countries.
practice.a: China produced the most rice of all countries.
Trains are generally faster than buses.

units.title: Advanced comparison: as…as, twice as, far more
units.summary: Precise comparisons with modifiers and multiples.

cards.title: Equality and multiples
cards.body: **as + adjective + as**, **not as … as**, **twice / three times as … as**, **half as many … as**.
examples: Japan spent twice as much as Korea.
Women were not as likely as men to cycle.
There were three times as many cars as in 1990.

cards.title: Modifying comparatives
cards.body: Big difference: **far, much, considerably, significantly** + comparative. Small difference: **slightly, a little, marginally**.
examples: Rents are far higher in the capital.
The figure was slightly lower in 2010.

cards.title: the … the …
cards.body: Two changes connected: **the more … , the more …**
examples: The more people drive, the worse the air becomes.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Precise comparisons are exactly what 'make comparisons where relevant' rewards.
examples: The USA consumed nearly three times as much energy per person as China.

practice.q: Prices in 2020 were ___ higher than in 2010.
Men were twice as likely ___ women to drive to work.
___ you practise, the more fluent you become.
The figure for France was [as same as] Italy's.
Rents are [very] higher in Dhaka than in Rajshahi.

o: Spain had half as many tourists as France.
Spain had half many tourists than France.
Spain had as half many tourists as France.
practice.a: Spain had half as many tourists as France.
The figure was slightly lower than in the previous year.

units.title: Adverbs of frequency and degree; word order
units.summary: Where adverbs go in a sentence.

cards.title: Frequency adverbs
cards.body: **always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, seldom, never** go **before the main verb** but **after be** and after the first auxiliary.
examples: I usually walk to work.
She is always late.
I have never been abroad.

cards.title: Degree adverbs
cards.body: **extremely, highly, quite, fairly, rather, slightly** go before adjectives and adverbs.
examples: It is highly unlikely.
The rise was fairly gradual.

cards.title: Don't split verb and object
cards.body: Do not put an adverb **between a verb and its object**.
examples: I speak English well. (not 'I speak well English')

items: I go always to the gym.
I always go to the gym.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Word-order errors with adverbs are frequent in Speaking Part 1. Get them right automatically.
examples: I rarely watch television these days; I mostly use streaming apps.

o: She is on time usually always.

practice.a: I usually study in the library.

units.title: -ed / -ing adjectives and adjective order
units.summary: bored or boring? And 'a beautiful old wooden house'.

cards.title: -ed and -ing
cards.body: **-ed** describes how a person **feels**; **-ing** describes the thing that **causes** the feeling.
examples: I was bored. The film was boring.
I'm interested in history. History is interesting.

cards.title: Order of adjectives
cards.body: Opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → purpose.
examples: a lovely small old house
a big red Italian sports car

items: I am very boring in class.
I am very bored in class.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Part 2 descriptions use several adjectives — the right order sounds natural.
examples: It was a small, family-run Thai restaurant with a really relaxing atmosphere.

practice.q: I felt ___ after the long journey.
Which is in the natural order?

practice.a: It was a beautiful old wooden house.

units.title: Prepositions of time
units.summary: in, on, at, by, until, during, for, since, from…to.

cards.title: in, on, at
cards.body: **in** + months, years, decades, seasons, parts of the day. **on** + days and dates. **at** + clock times, festivals, night, the weekend (UK).
examples: in 2010, in the 1990s, in July
on Monday, on 5 June
at 9 a.m., at night

cards.title: Periods
cards.body: **from … to / between … and** for a range; **during** + noun; **over** + period; **by** = not later than; **until** = up to a time.
examples: between 1990 and 2010
over the period
during the summer

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Task 1 depends on accurate time prepositions.
examples: Over the 20-year period, sales doubled, reaching a peak in 2015.

practice.q: The figure is expected to double ___ 2030.

practice.a: Car sales doubled over the period.

units.title: Prepositions of place and direction (maps)
units.summary: Describing location and change on maps and plans.

cards.title: Location
cards.body: **in** (an area), **on** (a surface or road), **at** (a point), **next to / beside / adjacent to**, **opposite**, **between**, **to the north of**, **in the south-east corner**.
examples: The school is on Station Road, opposite the park.
A hotel was built to the east of the lake.

cards.title: Movement
cards.body: **along, across, through, past, towards, into, out of**
examples: Walk along the river and go past the bridge.

items: in the north from the city
in the north of the city

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Map tasks in Writing Task 1 and Listening Section 2 depend on this language.
examples: The farmland in the north was replaced by a housing estate.

practice.q: The café is ___ the corner of the square.
A car park was built ___ the hospital.
The airport is located to the south [from] the city.
Walk ___ the park to reach the library.

practice.a: A new hotel was built opposite the beach.

units.title: Dependent prepositions
units.summary: Fixed combinations: depend on, interested in, the impact of… on…

items: the effect on X to Y
the effect of X on Y

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Wrong prepositions are among the most frequent errors in Task 2.
examples: Advertising has a strong influence on children's food choices.

practice.q: Parents are responsible ___ their children's safety.
We need a solution [for] traffic congestion.
Tourism has a big impact [to] local culture.

practice.a: Governments should invest in public transport.

units.title: The language of numbers and change
units.summary: rise to, rise by, stand at, peak at, account for — the core of Task 1.

cards.title: to, by, at, from
cards.body:
- **rose to 50%** (the new figure)
- **rose by 10%** (the amount of change)
- **stood at / was at 40%** (a single value)
- **peaked at / reached a peak of 80**
- **from 20 to 35** (start and end)
examples: The figure rose from 20% to 35%, an increase of 15 percentage points.
Coal accounted for 40% of electricity.

cards.title: Useful patterns
rows: Gas accounted for a third of the total.
a rise of X in Y

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Accurate figures with the right preposition are central to Task Achievement and Grammar.
examples: Renewables made up only 5% of the total in 2000 but rose to almost a fifth by 2020.

practice.q: Oil accounted [to] half of the energy used.
The number of visitors reached [to] a peak in July.

practice.a: Coal accounted for almost half of the electricity produced.
